open-question.question: Does the draft adopt the 2026-11-19 conversation's new-mission button, which takes a typed goal and opens an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session on it in a terminal, where the person carries the conversation on: as stated, in a refined form, or not at all? The draft's one way to start a mission today is the headless chain of the usage page, its `<goal>` and `<scope>` typed into an input box.
open-question.alternative: Adopted as stated: a new-mission button asks for the goal in an input box and opens a terminal running an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session with that goal as the skill's text, where the person carries the conversation on to its proposed goal and `--at` scope and runs `/define-mission-goal` from inside the session; the draft's existing button for the headless `define-mission-goal --at <scope> <goal>` line, its goal and scope typed into input boxes, stays beside it, so the draft names two ways to start a mission. It writes the maintainer's own start of every mission (the transcript's "you click it, you write the goal, ... you will continue the conversation there") into the draft unchanged, gets the scope proposal `discuss-mission-goal` makes from the `record .` read without the person working the scope out, and keeps the one-click headless definition for a goal that is already crisp. The typed goal lands inside the interactive line's quoted prompt, so the quoting rule of "Running a line" now covers free prose of any length, and the draft holds two start buttons whose difference it must explain; the button needs an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` line to exist, which depends on how the sibling question on where interactive lines come from settles, since `docs/ways-of-using.md` holds none.

Adopted as stated for the button itself (goal typed into an input box, an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session opened on it in a terminal, the person defining the mission from inside the session), and it replaces the draft's headless-definition button: the extension offers no button for the `define-mission-goal --at <scope> <goal>` line, `<goal>` and `<scope>` leave the placeholders the interface fills, and that line stays only on the usage page and in a person's own recipes. One way into a mission through the extension, the way the maintainer actually starts one, and the draft loses the scope input box, whose value a person typing it cold is the least placed to choose, since the definition invariant wants it as deep as the core allows and `discuss-mission-goal` is what proposes it. A person with a crisp goal and a known scope must go through a conversation, or paste the headless line by hand, to define a mission the draft's current button defines in one click, and the same quoting exposure for the typed goal and the same condition on the sibling question on interactive line sources apply.

Adopted in a refined form: the new-mission button takes no input and opens a terminal running an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session with no text, the person typing the goal as the conversation's first turn and defining the mission from inside the session; the draft's headless-definition button with its goal and scope input boxes stays beside it. The goal is typed once, into the session that reasons over it, rather than into an input box whose text is then quoted into a command line, so no free prose of the person's passes through the line's quoting at all and the button's line is fixed text with no placeholder at all, while the quick headless definition stays available. It departs from the conversation's stated flow (type the goal, press enter, land in the terminal) by one step, and the person still meets two start buttons; it still needs an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` line from wherever the sibling question on interactive line sources places them.

Adopted in a refined form that also replaces the draft's headless-definition button: the one start button takes no input and opens a terminal running an interactive `discuss-mission-goal` session with no text, the person typing the goal there and defining the mission from inside the session, and the extension offers no button for the `define-mission-goal --at <scope> <goal>` line, which stays on the usage page and in a person's own recipes. The smallest interface of the adopting options: one fixed line with no placeholder of the person's own text, no goal or scope input box anywhere in the extension, and no quoting exposure for a mission's start. It removes the one-click definition the draft already has and departs from the stated typed-goal flow at once, so both a crisp-goal start and the transcript's own description are served less directly; it still rests on the sibling question on interactive line sources for its line.

Dropped from the draft for good, listed among the dropped ideas with a one-line reason: the extension gets no new-mission button for `discuss-mission-goal`, its one way to start a mission stays the headless `define-mission-goal --at <scope> <goal>` line with its two input boxes, and a person who wants the discussion runs `/discuss-mission-goal` by hand in a terminal of their own, as the snippet file's bare slash commands have it today. The draft keeps its present scope with no new interactive line to source, no free-text quoting case added, and nothing more for a first version to build, and starting a mission is rare beside the answering and execution sittings the extension mainly exists for. The step the maintainer begins every mission with stays hand work outside the extension, and the headless button asks for a scope the person must choose without the record read `discuss-mission-goal` makes, which invites the root or another over-wide placement the definition invariant warns against.

open-question.question: Does the draft adopt the 2026-11-19 conversation's one pane with a page per mission, on which a mission's questions, tasks, and buttons stand together, and if so does it replace the draft's side-bar tree of missions and its custom editor claiming `open_questions.xml`, or stand beside either? The draft's VS Code check names no pane other than the custom editor.
open-question.alternative: The draft does not adopt the per-mission page: it keeps its two parts as written, the side-bar tree of live missions with their open questions and remaining task headings beneath each, where the recipe buttons hang, and the read-only custom editor claiming `open_questions.xml` as the question view with the per-question buttons. The pane is listed among the dropped ideas with a one-line reason. Nothing in the draft's parts changes, and the one surface the question view rests on, the custom editor claimed by a file-name glob, is the one the draft's VS Code check already covers. It drops the experience the 2026-11-19 conversation centres on, a mission's questions, tasks, and buttons standing together on one state-aware page, and leaves the mission-level buttons on a tree the draft itself says adds little to `missions.py live` as a display.

The draft adopts the pane as stated: one pane in the editor area, holding one page per live mission and a way on the pane itself to move between missions, each page showing that mission's state, its open questions, its remaining tasks, and every button, the per-question ones included. It replaces both the side-bar tree and the custom editor: the extension contributes no tree and claims no file, so `open_questions.xml` opened from the explorer shows its XML text. One surface to build and describe, exactly the form the conversation proposes, with every button of a mission in one place and no second rendering of the same questions to keep in step. Opening the question document from the explorer brings back the raw, entity-escaped XML the draft measured as hard to read, only one mission's page is in view at a time although two missions' chains may run at once, and the pane rests on an editor-area panel the draft's VS Code check never covered (a condition on the further-checks question).

The draft adopts the one pane with a page per mission, carrying the questions, tasks, and buttons, and keeps the side-bar tree of live missions as the way into it: selecting a mission in the tree opens or switches the pane to that mission's page. The custom editor claiming `open_questions.xml` is dropped, the questions being shown only on the page. The live missions stay listed in the side bar, always in view and one click from their page, while the questions are still rendered in one place only. The tree and the page list the same questions and task headings unless the tree is cut to missions alone, the question document opened from the explorer shows raw XML, and both surfaces rest on parts the draft's check left unchecked, the side-bar tree and the editor-area panel (a condition on the further-checks question).

alternative.id: One pane beside the question editor

open-question.alternative: The draft adopts the one pane with a page per mission, carrying the questions, tasks, and buttons, and drops the side-bar tree, the pane holding its own way to move between missions. The custom editor claiming `open_questions.xml` stays beside it, so opening the document from the explorer shows the same question rendering the page shows. The question document reads rendered however it is reached, from the pane or from the file, which keeps the draft's original fix for the raw XML while the transcript's page becomes the working surface. The same questions are rendered on two surfaces whose buttons and refresh after a run must stay in step, a double cost whichever renderer the question-renderer question settles on, and the pane itself is outside what the draft's check covered.

The draft adopts the one pane with a page per mission, carrying the questions, tasks, and buttons, and keeps both of its parts beside it: the side-bar tree of live missions as the way into the pages, and the custom editor claiming `open_questions.xml` so the document opened from the explorer is still rendered. Every way a person might reach a mission or its questions, the side bar, the pane, or the file, leads to a rendered view, so nothing the draft offered is lost by adding the page. Three surfaces to build and keep consistent, two of them rendering the same questions and the tree repeating the page's lists, the largest cost of the set for an experiment whose first user is the maintainer, and two of the three rest on parts the draft's check left unchecked.

The draft adopts a page per mission in a refined form: the custom editor claiming `open_questions.xml` is widened into the mission page, showing beside the questions the mission's state, its remaining tasks, and every button, so each mission's page is its own editor tab opened by opening its question document, as a Markdown preview is opened, rather than one pane switching pages. The side-bar tree is dropped, the explorer being the way in. It realizes the page on the one surface the draft's VS Code check already covered, behaves like the preview the conversation names as its model, and lets two missions' pages stand open side by side while their chains run at once. The extension lists no live missions of its own, so a page is reached only by finding `mission_<slug>/open_questions.xml` in the explorer, and an editor claimed by the question document shows content the file does not hold, the task list and the mission's state.

The draft adopts a page per mission in the same refined form, the custom editor claiming `open_questions.xml` widened into the mission page with its state, questions, remaining tasks, and buttons, one editor tab per mission, and keeps the side-bar tree of live missions as the way in: selecting a mission in the tree opens its question document in that editor. Each mission's page is a tab of its own on the already-checked custom editor, so two pages stand side by side, and the side bar still lists the live missions so no page needs finding in the explorer. Two parts to build, the tree repeating the page's lists unless it is cut to missions alone, the side-bar tree still unchecked (a condition on the further-checks question), and the claimed editor still shows content its file does not hold.

The draft adopts a page per mission refined into the side bar: a view in the side bar, in place of the tree, shows the selected mission's page, its state, its questions as headings with their picks, its remaining task headings, and the mission-level buttons, while the custom editor claiming `open_questions.xml` is kept in the editor area for reading a question whole, with its per-question buttons. The mission's state and buttons stay in view beside the editor area and the terminal while a question is read in full in a wide editor, so the page never competes with the run it starts for the main area. The page is split across two surfaces, the side bar being too narrow for alternatives in full, so it holds only if questions are shown collapsed to their headings (a condition on the heading-first screening question), and a side-bar view other than a tree is outside the draft's check.

open-question.question: Which states of a mission does the extension tell apart, from what does it read them, and does a state only show or also decide which buttons are offered: the `started` or `defined` of `missions.py live` with the open-question and task lists, or the finer states `ideas/kepala.md` names (Scoped through Done), which that draft reads from the last run's fixed first line?

Does the draft adopt the 2026-11-19 conversation's proposal that the extension carry out task completion itself, running the `complete-task` skill once per remaining task in list order in place of the one `complete-all-tasks` line, so that each task can run under its own host, model, and effort: as stated, in a refined form, or not at all? The draft's constraint has the extension hold no skill order of its own.

When tasks are run one at a time, how is each task's host, model, and effort chosen, and where is what that choice needs kept: picked by the person per task, taken from assignments or rules kept in the project as the 2026-11-19 conversation proposes, or assigned by a model run reading each brief? A task section holds a title and a brief with no field for a kind of work, the maintainer's largest mission held about 140 tasks, and the draft's constraint has the extension write nothing under a mission directory.
open-question.alternative: No per-task choice now: a task run uses one host, model, and effort for every task, chosen once per run, as `complete-all-tasks` does today. A task that needs another profile is run by hand through the snippet file's single-task line. Nothing is kept anywhere. The draft lists per-task assignment as a later question rather than ruling it out for good. Nothing new to design, store, or keep in step with the task list. The constraint stands untouched, and a person who wants Fable or `agy` for one task already can, with the single-task line. It drops the capability the transcript names as the reason to build the extension, that a 140-task mission runs its few model-generation tasks under Fable or `agy` and the hundred others under a cheaper profile, so the person stays the orchestrator for every exception.

The person chooses each task's host, model, and effort in the extension before or during the run, from a list of the remaining tasks with one run-wide default preselected. The choices are held in memory for that run only. They are written to no file and no extension storage, and a new run starts again from the default. It is the smallest form of per-task choice. Nothing is written under a mission directory or anywhere else, nothing can go stale against renamed or completed tasks, and the person sees every assignment before it spends tokens. The assignments are lost when the editor closes or a run stops part way, and the draft's decided rule that a run lives no longer than the editor makes that common on long runs. On a 140-task list the person has to re-pick every exception each time, which is the hand work the extension exists to remove.

alternative.id: Person picks, kept in extension storage

open-question.alternative: The person chooses each task's profile in the extension, defaulting to one run-wide profile. The extension keeps each choice in its own private workspace storage, outside the repository, keyed by the mission path and the task title, and offers it again on the next run or resume. The choices survive an editor restart and a stopped run, and still nothing is written into the project, so the constraint and every plugin invariant hold. The choices are private to one machine and one person, invisible to a collaborator and to anyone running the pasted lines, and versioned nowhere. Keying by title breaks when a task is renamed and can attach an old choice to a reused title, and 140 tasks still need one pick each.

alternative.id: Assignment table in a project file

open-question.alternative: The person's per-task choices are kept as explicit assignments, mission path plus task title mapped to a host, model, and effort, in a tracked file outside every mission directory (for example under the extension's own project-level configuration). The extension writes the file when the person picks, any task without an entry gets the file's default profile, and the file can be edited by hand. The assignments are versioned and shared with collaborators, survive anything that ends a run, and are exact, so no task is classified wrongly without the person having written it so. The extension starts writing into the project, outside mission directories but against the spirit of a pure line runner. Entries are keyed by titles that the task list removes on completion and may reuse, so the table grows stale with nothing to prune it, and 140 tasks still mean one entry per exception.

alternative.id: Project rules over title and brief

open-question.alternative: Rules kept in a tracked project file outside every mission directory map patterns over a task's title and brief text (keywords or regular expressions, for example "model generation" or "animation") to a host, model, and effort, with a default profile for tasks no rule matches. The extension evaluates them before each task, shows the resulting assignment, and lets the person override a task for the current run only, the override kept nowhere. This is the "state in the project that auto-assigns models" the 2026-11-19 conversation proposes. A handful of rules covers a 140-task mission with no per-task work, applies to every later mission in the project, and is versioned and shared. It needs no change to the plugin or its task format. A brief is one to three free sentences with no field for a kind of work, so pattern matching is fuzzy. A wording the rules did not foresee silently puts a task on the default profile, or a broad rule silently puts the hundred ordinary tasks on Fable and drains the tokens the scheme exists to save.

The same pattern rules over title and brief, with a default profile and per-run overrides kept nowhere, but kept in the person's own user-level editor settings rather than in the project, so they follow the person across projects and are never committed. Which hosts and models are usable is personal: an `agy` subscription and a token budget belong to the person, not the project. Personal rules never push one collaborator's subscriptions onto another, and nothing at all is written into the repository. The matching is as fuzzy as with project rules, and the rules are not versioned with the work, so two people running one mission assign it differently. A project's own kinds of work, such as its model-generation tasks, have to be re-described in every person's settings.

alternative.id: Kind marker in the task brief

open-question.alternative: The task format gains an optional kind-of-work marker, a short word in a fixed position of the brief or title, that `derive-tasks` and `submit-task` write when they author a task and the task-list tool stores as text. A tracked project file outside every mission directory maps each kind to a host, model, and effort, with a default for unmarked tasks. The extension reads the marker and the mapping and still writes nothing under a mission directory, since the plugin's own skills write the marker. The classification is made once, by the run that already reads the requirements and authors the task, so it is deliberate rather than guessed from wording. It travels with the task into its `Task-completion:` commit, and the mapping stays a small, shared file of a few kinds. It changes the plugin for the extension, which the constraint says needs no plugin change. It also breaks the task-altitude rule that a section is only a title and a one-to-three-sentence brief with no other field, and every task authored before the change, plus every mission on a plugin copy without it, carries no marker.

Before the task loop, the extension runs one headless model call over the remaining task list. It reads each title and brief against a tracked project file outside every mission directory that describes the available profiles (for example "visual or model-generation work: `agy` with Gemini"), and the call proposes a host, model, and effort for every task. The person confirms or overrides the proposals in the extension. The confirmed assignments are kept in the extension's private workspace storage, keyed by mission path and task title, so a resume does not classify again. It reads free-text briefs the way a person would, so it handles wording no keyword rule foresaw. It needs no task-format change, and a 140-task list is assigned in one call with the person reviewing rather than authoring each pick. Every execution pays an extra model run whose output is nondeterministic. The extension has to hold a prompt of its own rather than only the lines a person would type, which is against the constraint, unless that prompt ships as a new plugin skill, which is a plugin change. Its viability also depends on how the Kepala boundary question places automatic decisions.

open-question.question: When a task runs under a host, model, and effort chosen for it, is its command line one of the recipe file's own single-task lines picked by name, so the extension still holds no host flag, model name, or effort level of its own, or does the extension compose the line from the three values and so hold each host's command syntax?
open-question.alternative: The recipe file holds complete single-task lines, one per host, model, and effort combination wanted, each under a name of its own and each in the form the snippet file already has (`claude -p "/gurita:complete-task --mission <path> <Task Title>" ... --model "opus" --effort xhigh`, `agy -p ... --model "claude-opus-5-5" --effort high`). A task's chosen combination is a reference to one of those names; the extension picks the named line and fills only `<path>` and `<Task Title>`. It holds no host flag, model name, or effort level, and "The constraint" and the Recipes part stand as written. Keeps the draft's constraint exactly as it stands, with every host's syntax only as text in lines a person can paste and run by hand, the way the snippet file's two single-task lines already run today, so nothing new enters the extension and no host change can break code of its own. Every combination used is a line to write and keep, so lines multiply with hosts times models times efforts and a combination nobody wrote cannot be chosen; the choice of a task's run becomes a choice of a line name, which holds only if the way per-task assignments are kept (the per-task assignment question's axis) can name a line rather than three values.

The recipe file holds one single-task line per host with two new placeholders beside `<path>` and `<Task Title>`, such as `<model>` and `<effort>`, in the positions that host's flags take (`--model "<model>" --effort <effort>` on Claude Code and Antigravity; on Codex `-m "<model>"` and no effort position, since it has no effort flag). The chosen host picks the template, and the extension substitutes the chosen model and effort as plain values the way it fills any placeholder; the host's command syntax stays text in the recipe, while the model and effort values come from wherever the task's choice is kept rather than from the extension's code. The notation gains the two placeholders. Any model and effort a host accepts can be chosen with one line per host, so the line count stays at the number of hosts while the extension still holds no host flag syntax and every template remains a pasteable line. Adds two placeholders to the recipe notation and a rule for a template that lacks a position (Codex's effort, silently ignored), and a value the host refuses (an `xhigh` on `agy`, a model id written in another host's form) surfaces only as that run's stop, since nothing checks the value against the host before the run; how far the draft's "no model name or effort level" wording must be reworded depends on where the per-task assignment question keeps the values.

The extension builds each single-task line from the three values itself: it holds, per host, the binary and headless form (`claude -p`, `agy -p`, `codex exec`), the prompt's sigil and quoting (`"/gurita:..."` against `'$gurita:...'`), the permission flag, and the model and effort flags (`--model`/`--effort`, Codex's `-m` with no effort), the rules the legend of `docs/ways-of-using.md` states for moving a line between hosts. The recipe file holds no single-task line, and "The constraint" and the Recipes part are rewritten to say the extension holds each host's command syntax for this one line. Any host, model, and effort combination runs with no line written by anyone, and the extension can check a combination before the run (Antigravity's `high` ceiling, Codex's missing effort flag) and offer only the values each host takes. Puts a second copy of each host's command syntax in the extension's code beside the legend, which drifts when a host renames a flag or a model id form, and breaks the draft's constraint that all host-specific text lives in lines a person could type, so the composed line is no longer one a recipe file shows or a person can edit.

A stdlib-only tool added to the plugin's tools takes a host, model, effort, mission path, and task title and prints the complete headless `complete-task` line for that host; the extension runs it from the plugin's installed copy and executes what it prints, holding no host syntax itself, while the per-host rules move from the legend's prose into that tested tool, which the legend may then describe. The draft's "no plugin change" consequence is rewritten. Gives the host syntax one tested home shipped with the plugin that knows its own hosts, so the extension and any other runner, Kepala included, compose the same line without holding a copy of their own. Turns a draft for an extension into a plugin change, a fifth tool kind (one that prints commands for other hosts) the plugin has never had, and needs the plugin's installed location found per host, which stays open under the live-state question; the line it prints is still invisible to a person until it runs.

The revision does not settle the line's source now: it lists, among the draft's questions for the work, whether a per-task line is a named recipe line, a per-host template, or composed, with those options written out, and the Recipes part and "The constraint" stay as written until the work answers it. Keeps the revision from fixing a mechanism before per-task running and its assignment have been tried, at the cost of nothing the draft says today. Leaves an adopted per-task loop with no stated way to build its lines, so the draft describes a feature whose one host-facing step is open and whose fit with its own constraint is unknown; it holds only if the task-loop question adopts the loop in some form, and is moot otherwise.

open-question.question: Where the extension orders runs itself (a task loop, a bounded repeat), how does the draft place that logic against the orchestrator `ideas/kepala.md` outlines: as the interface-independent part Kepala may reuse, as a first form of Kepala itself, or left out, with all automatic ordering kept for Kepala? The draft's Kepala section calls its runner Kepala's transition engine with a person choosing the edge.
open-question.alternative: Whatever ordering the extension does (the task loop, a bounded repeat) sits in the part the draft already keeps apart from the VS Code interface, beside the recipes, the fixed-line reading, and the state read. The Kepala section is rewritten so that the runner walks only the edges a recipe names (the `Listed` self-loop task by task, the review repeated until its verdict line), with the person choosing every other edge. Whether Kepala reuses that part stays Kepala's question, as the section says today. It extends the separation the draft already draws, so the section changes by one sentence, and it makes no claim on Kepala's design, which `ideas/kepala.md` says is settled in the work itself and holds nothing decided. The ordering logic is held to an interface-free design for a reuse that may never come, with the maintainer as its one consumer, and "may reuse" commits Kepala to nothing, so the duplication it guards against is still possible. It has something to place only if the extension-run task loop or the recipe bounded repeat is adopted.

The draft names the extension's ordering part an early Kepala: the transition engine of `ideas/kepala.md`'s state diagram walking the subset of its edges the extension automates (the task self-loop, the review repeat), with the extension as that engine's interface at the `Recommended` state and the person choosing the edges it does not walk. The Kepala section says the part is Kepala's start rather than something Kepala may reuse. There is one engine rather than two: the per-task host, model, and effort work the transcript wants delivered now goes straight into the orchestrator, and nothing has to be rewritten once Kepala is built. It settles part of Kepala's design from this draft, while `ideas/kepala.md` plans the orchestrator in its own repository and around a cross-mission Definition-of-Done loop that a per-mission button runner does not cover. The two drafts then disagree unless `ideas/kepala.md` is revised as well, which this mission's goal does not name. Its viability also turns on where the extension's code lives and on whether a task loop or bounded repeat is adopted at all.

The ordering logic lives in the extension beside its interface, and no interface-free part is claimed for it. The recipes, fixed-line reading, and state read stay separated as the draft has them. The draft draws the boundary by scope instead of by reuse: the extension orders the runs of one mission's one chain, started by a person's click, while Kepala orders missions toward a Definition of Done. The Kepala section's sentence calling the runner Kepala's transition engine is dropped. It is the simplest build with no abstraction made ahead of need, and the boundary it states (within one mission vs. across missions) follows the line between `ideas/kepala.md`'s outer loop and its inner states. A Kepala built later writes its own task loop and run-outcome reading again, a second copy of how a run's end is read, and the draft gives up the link to Kepala it states today. It has something to place only if the extension-run task loop or the recipe bounded repeat is adopted.

The extension orders nothing itself: each button runs its recipe's lines as given, the person chooses every edge, and the draft states that all automatic ordering, a task loop and a bounded repeat included, belongs to Kepala. The Recipes part's "no skill order of its own" and the Kepala section stand as written. The extension stays a thin interface over the pasted lines, with "The constraint" unchanged and no overlap with Kepala to manage, so ordering logic is written once, in the orchestrator. Per-task host, model, and effort, the feature the transcript most wants delivered, waits on an orchestrator that has nothing decided and no work planned. This option holds together only if the extension-run task loop and the recipe bounded repeat are both not adopted.

The revised draft does not settle the boundary now. It lists, among its questions for the work, how any ordering the extension does relates to Kepala, and the Kepala section's sentence on the runner is narrowed to the parts the draft already keeps interface-free, saying nothing about who orders runs. Nothing is promised about an orchestrator whose design is still open, and the choice is made once the extension's ordering exists in code and can be compared with a real Kepala outline. The design draft leaves its main structural link unstated, so whoever builds the ordering has no rule for which side of the line it goes on, and the code written first will settle the boundary by default.

open-question.question: Where do the interactive command lines behind the extension's buttons come from, the `discuss-open-question` session the question view opens and any `discuss-mission-goal` session a new-mission button opens, given that `docs/ways-of-using.md` holds only headless lines and the draft has the extension hold no host flag or model name of its own?

Does the question view show each question collapsed to its title and its pick until the person opens it, to fit the maintainer's report that most questions are screened by their heading alone and only one or two are read in full, or does it show every question whole as the draft describes?
open-question.alternative: The question view stays as the draft's Question view part describes it: every question is shown whole and open, with its question text, its pick and rationale, every alternative with its what-it-is, advantage, and drawback, its dependencies, and its applied principles. There is no collapsed form and no collapse control. The maintainer's heading-first screening is left to scrolling, and the draft's Question view text is not changed. Nothing is added to the view or to the draft: one rendering, nothing hidden behind a click, and every alternative's record button visible at once for the person who does read a question in full. It fits the reading the maintainer reports least well: most questions are passed over by their heading, so a document of twenty-odd questions with several alternatives each is mostly scrolled past, which is the hand work the extension exists to cut.

Each question is shown collapsed by default to one row holding its Short Title and the id of its picked alternative (no pick shown when it carries none). The question-level buttons (discuss, answer in the person's own words, record the recommendation) stand on the row; opening the row shows the question whole as the draft describes, with the alternative buttons inside it. The view carries expand-all and collapse-all controls. The draft's Question view part is rewritten to say so. It is the shape the maintainer's report describes: the heading decides whether the question matters, and the pick's id beside it says what will be recorded if nothing is done, so a question is opened only to disagree. An option id alone may not say what the pick does, so judging whether the recommendation is fine can still mean opening the question; and the collapsed rendering needs a fold the renderer supports, which depends on what the Question document renderer question settles.
